html:
A woodblock print by the Japanese artist Hokusai, made in late 1831 in Edo-period Japan. A huge wave curls like a claw over three boats of rowers, while Mount Fuji sits small in the distance. It is the best-known image in Japanese art.

It was the first print in Hokusai's series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. He was over seventy when he made it. Like other ukiyo-e prints, it was cheap and made in large runs: an artist drew the design, carvers cut it into wooden blocks, one per colour, and printers inked and pressed sheets by hand. Thousands of copies were printed, which is why museums around the world own one.

Two things stand out:

  • It uses Prussian blue, a synthetic pigment newly imported through the Dutch trade, which gave a deep, lasting colour.
  • It borrows Western perspective, with a low horizon and a far-off Fuji, a style Hokusai had learned from European prints.

When Japan opened to the world after 1853, prints like this reached Europe in large numbers. They set off Japonisme. Painters such as Van Gogh, Monet and Degas collected them and copied their flat colours, bold outlines and unusual angles, and the first edition of Debussy's La Mer put it on the cover. The wave is still everywhere today, from posters to emoji.
